intro: A normalization layer need not subtract the mean. Inspect what happens to a constant nonzero activation when you scale by its root mean square instead.
task: Implement RMS normalization along the last axis and apply one learned weight per feature. Compare the result with the centering operation in layer normalization.
requirements: x has one or more dimensions, all nonempty; weight has shape (x.shape[-1],). Return a new NumPy array with the same shape as x.
Compute sqrt(mean(x**2, axis=-1, keepdims=True) + eps). Divide x by this denominator, then multiply by weight. Do not subtract a mean.
eps is a positive real scalar; epsilon belongs inside the square root.
Inputs must be real numeric values with finite magnitude at most 1e30. Leave inputs unchanged and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

hints.title: Keep the reduced axis
hints.body: Retain a length-one last axis in the mean so the denominator broadcasts back over every feature.

hints.title: Test a constant row
hints.body: A positive constant row should stay positive. Mean subtraction would turn it into zeros.

explanation: RMS normalization controls activation scale while preserving a nonzero mean. For a row of identical positive values, the normalized result is close to one before applying weights.
The last-axis reduction treats each earlier index independently. A learned weight can change both magnitude and sign, so the weighted output need not have RMS one.
This NumPy adaptation keeps the upstream forward computation. It adds explicit input validation and independent examples; it does not implement PyTorch autograd.
